newsitem.title: USA: EU's Brittan meets US lawmakers on Helms-Burton.
newsitem.headline: EU's Brittan meets US lawmakers on Helms-Burton.

text.p: European Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan met U.S. lawmakers on Tuesday to discuss a pending settlement of a dispute with the United States over a U.S. law aimed at curbing foreign investment in Cuba.

Brittan told reporters at a news conference that the agreement reached last month with U.S. Commerce Undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat was "not a solution to the problem, but has defused it and is a launch pad for further progress."

Under the agreement, the EU agreed to set aside its challenge against the so-called Helms-Burton law in the World Trade Organization, while the United States and European Union worked out a common policy on properties seized by the communist government in Cuba after Fidel Castro took power in 1959.

The United States agreed to continue waiving a provision of the law that allows U.S. citizens to sue investors who profit from seized property and to seek a change in another key provision of the law.

That provision bars executives of companies investing in confiscated property from entering the United States. The change would allow President Clinton to waive that provision as well as the lawsuit provision.

Brittan said it was useful to be able to explain the understanding to lawmakers, who would have to vote on the proposed change to the legislation. The law was enacted last year after the Cuban government shot down two U.S. civilian aircraft being flown by anti-Castro activists.
The EU trade chief met a number of U.S. lawmakers including Sen. Paul Coverdell, R-Ga., who heads the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on Western Hemisphere.
He also met Eizenstat, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, and White House economic policy adviser Gene Sperling.

Brittan said he also discussed with lawmakers Europe's objections to a U.S. law that punishes foreign companies that invest $40 million or more a year in Iranian or Libyan oil and gas projects and the need to address that as part of the settlement of the dispute over the Helms-Burton law
He said he thought there ought to be a waiver for Europe under that law since it shares U.S. concerns about terrorism.
